name: Miyamoto Musashi
title: The Master
tagline: He gave his whole life to one craft, then wrote down how, so others could learn.

story.title: A boy and a duel
story.text: Musashi was born in Japan around 1584. At about thirteen he fought his first duel, against a trained swordsman named Arima Kihei, and won. Accounts differ on his exact age.

story.title: The long road
story.text: He spent years travelling and testing himself against others. Accounts credit him with around sixty duels without a defeat.

story.title: The island
story.text: In 1612 he faced the famous swordsman Sasaki Kojiro on Ganryu Island. Tradition says he carved a wooden sword from a boat oar on the way there. Historians disagree on how the duel really went.

story.title: Two swords as one
story.text: He created his own style, using the long and the short sword together. It is still taught today as Niten Ichi-ryu.

story.title: The brush
story.text: The swordsman was also an ink painter and calligrapher. Works such as Shrike Perched on a Withered Branch are attributed to him.

story.title: The cave
story.text: In 1643 he withdrew to the Reigando cave near Kumamoto and wrote The Book of Five Rings, finished in 1645. About a week before he died, he wrote the Dokkodo: 21 short precepts for life.

principles.title: Build on solid ground
principles.idea: The Earth book compares strategy to building a house: master the basics and the practical principles first, and everything else stands on them.

quote.text: Know the smallest things and the biggest things.
quote.credit: The Book of Five Rings, Earth book, tr. Victor Harris (1974)

principles.practice: Pick one skill you care about. Write down its three basics and practise one of them for 15 minutes.

principles.title: Be like water
principles.idea: The Water book is about flexibility: a balanced body and mind that can adapt to whatever comes, instead of freezing in one fixed stance.
principles.practice: When something goes off-plan today, don't fight it. Write one line on how you adapted.

principles.title: Master your timing
principles.idea: The Fire book teaches timing and rhythm: read the situation, choose your position, and act before the moment passes.
principles.practice: Do your hardest task at the hour you think most clearly, before anything else can take that time.

principles.title: Learn other ways
principles.idea: In the Wind book Musashi studies rival schools, arguing that you must understand another person's way to master your own.
principles.practice: Spend 20 minutes learning how someone in a completely different field solves the problem you are working on.

principles.title: Don't chase an easy life
principles.idea: Among the Dokkodo precepts he wrote at the end of his life is a warning against seeking comfort for its own sake.

quote.text: Don't try and look for an easy life.

principles.practice: Once today, when there is an easy option and a better option, choose the better one.

challenge.title: Solid ground
challenge.action: Pick one skill. List its three basics. Practise one for 15 minutes.

challenge.title: Like water
challenge.action: When something goes off-plan, adapt instead of complaining. Write one line about how.

challenge.title: Timing
challenge.action: Do your hardest task at your sharpest hour, before email or social media.

challenge.title: Other ways
challenge.action: Spend 20 minutes learning how another field solves your problem.

challenge.title: The harder path
challenge.action: Choose the better option over the easy one, once.

challenge.title: No regrets
challenge.action: Write down one past mistake and the lesson in it. Then let it go.

challenge.title: Your own rule
challenge.action: Repeat day 1's practice and notice what improved. Write your own rule for life in one line.

reflect: Which of the five principles would change the most in your life if you practised it every day for a year?
